title: The Dirt of the State

zh.text: 天下莫柔弱於水，而攻堅強者，莫之能勝，其無以易之。

gloss.2: none, nothing (the graph first pictured dusk)
gloss.6: water; the Shuowen says: the level
gloss.9: to attack, to lay siege to
gloss.17: to overcome, to get the better of
gloss.22: yì: to replace, to exchange; also “to change” and “easy”

zh.text: 弱之勝強，柔之勝剛，天下莫不知莫能行。是以聖人云﹕「受國之垢，是謂社稷主；受國不祥，是為天下王。」正言若反。

gloss.8: hard, unbending (of metal, of a blade)
gloss.17: to walk it, to carry it out
gloss.26: to receive, to take into one’s hands
gloss.34: jì: millet; the altar of grain
gloss.35: lord, host; first, the flame of a lamp
gloss.40: auspicious; 不祥: things of ill omen

rendering: Under heaven nothing is softer and weaker than [[water|shui]],
yet for [[attacking|gong]] the hard and strong
[[there is nothing to put in its place|yi]].
Under heaven [[no one does not know this;|mo]]
is to be called [[lord of the altars of soil and grain|sheji]].
To take on the state’s [[ill omens|bu-xiang]]
is to be [[king of all under heaven|wang]].”

sheng.title: 聖人: not a saint
sheng.body: 聖人 is “the sage” by custom, and the English word misleads. This is not a saint: there is no holiness here and no reward after death. It is not only a wise man either. The graph has 耳, an ear, and the Shuowen defines the word as 通, “to pass through, to reach”: a person whose hearing is open, and who leads by that attunement. Here a sage is quoted on what makes a ruler. For early readers the sages were first of all the kings of old, and the saying that follows is about one of their acts.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 耳部: 聖，通也。从耳呈聲。

shui.title: 水: the level
shui.body: The Shuowen does not define water as wet. Its definition is one word: 凖也, “it is the level”. Water is the thing that finds the horizontal, and builders used a trough of it to set a line true. This fits the passage before this one, where heaven’s way is to bring the high down and the low up. The dictionary then reads the graph: 象眾水並流，中有微陽之气也, “it pictures many waters that flow side by side, with a faint breath of yang in the middle”. The centre line of 水 is the current; the strokes at the sides are the waters that join it. Water has been the book’s teacher since passage 8: the highest good is like water, which benefits all things and stays in the places that people despise. Here the lesson is the last one, and the hardest: what water’s low place means for a ruler.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 水部: 水，凖也。北方之行。象眾水並流，中有微陽之气也。

gong.title: 攻: water at the walls
gong.body: 攻 is the word for an assault on a fortified place; the Shuowen says 擊也, to strike. For a reader of the Warring States, “water attacks the hard and strong” was also a report of events. Cities had walls of rammed earth, and generals learned to turn rivers against them. In 453 BCE Zhi Bo led a river into Jinyang until the people hung their cooking pots from the rafters. In 279 BCE the Qin general Bai Qi dug a channel and drowned the Chu city of Yan. In 225 BCE Wang Ben of Qin breached the dikes above Daliang, the capital of Wei; after three months the walls dissolved and the state was at an end. The Sunzi notes dryly: 以水佐攻者強, “those who use water to support an attack are strong”. So the soft thing was a siege engine. The passage knows this and goes past it.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 攴部: 攻，擊也。从攴工聲。
Shiji 73, “Bai Qi Wang Jian liezhuan”; Shiji 6, “Qin Shihuang benji”
Shuijing zhu 28, “Mian shui” (the flooding of Yan)

yi.title: 易: replace, change, or easy?
yi.body: 其無以易之 turns on 易, a word with three senses. Wang Bi takes “to replace”: 以，用也。其，謂水也。言用水之柔弱，無物可以易之也。 “以 means to use. 其 refers to water. The line says: for the use of water’s softness and weakness, there is no thing that can take its place.” We follow him. A second sense is “to change”: nothing can alter water. Cut it, block it, boil it, and it comes back as itself. This reading explains the victory: the attacker that cannot be changed outlasts the wall that can. A third sense is “easy”, and a few readers take the line so: water treats nothing as easy. A modern collated edition of the Mawangdui silk texts begins the clause with 以, “because”, which makes it plainly the reason for the lines before. All three senses belong to one word, and the calligraphy plate for 易 below tells its story.

gang.title: Four words, re-paired
gang.body: The first sentence joins the qualities in two compounds: 柔弱, soft-weak, and 堅強, hard-strong. The second sentence takes them apart and sets them in single combat: 弱 against 強, 柔 against 剛. 剛 is new. It is the hardness of metal; the Shuowen defines it as 彊斷也, “to cut through by force”, and the graph has 刂, a knife, on its right. With 柔 it makes one of the great pairs of Chinese thought: in the Book of Changes, 剛 and 柔 are the names of the unbroken and the broken line. A modern collated edition of the Mawangdui silk texts has a different first clause: 水之勝剛, “water’s overcoming of the hard”. There the image stays on the surface for one more line. Passage 36 gives the same thought in four characters: 柔弱勝剛強. The saying was already old, and that is the point of the next line.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 刀部: 剛，彊斷也。从刀岡聲。

mo.title: 莫, four times: no one, nothing
mo.body: The passage is built on 莫, “none”. Nothing is softer than water. Nothing can beat it. No one does not know. No one can do it. The graph began as a picture of dusk; the Shuowen says 日且冥也。从日在茻中, “the sun about to go dark: a sun in the middle of tall grass”. It was borrowed for the negative, and a new graph, 暮, was made for the evening. The third and fourth 莫 make the most honest sentence in the book: 莫不知，莫能行. Everyone knows; no one can walk it. 行 is to walk, to put the feet on the road. Passage 70 said the same of the whole teaching: my words are very easy to know and very easy to walk, and no one under heaven can know them or walk them. Why is this knowledge so hard to walk? The quotation that follows gives the reason: the price is [[dirt|gou]].
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 茻部: 莫，日且冥也。从日在茻中。

yun.title: A verse inside the prose
yun.body: 聖人云, “a sage has said”. The author steps back and quotes; the same formula introduces a saying in passage 57. The four lines that follow are a small poem, and they rhyme. In the sound system reconstructed for Old Chinese, 垢 and 主 end in the same rhyme, the group that the tradition calls 侯, and 祥 and 王 share another, the group called 陽. Modern Mandarin has lost the first pair (gòu, zhǔ) and kept the second (xiáng, wáng). So dirt rhymes with lord, and ill omen rhymes with king. The ear joins what the mind keeps apart. The verse is probably older than the book: a court saying about what makes a ruler, which the author found and set here as the answer to “no one can walk it”. The Chinese has no “a” or “the”, so 聖人 can also be “the sages”.

shou.title: 受: from hand to hand
shou.body: 受 is to receive. The Shuowen defines it as 相付也, “to hand over to one another”, and builds it from two hands, one above and one below, with a reduced 舟, boat, between them for the sound. The early forms are commonly explained as two hands and a vessel that passes from one to the other. In early writing the one graph served for giving and for getting; later a hand was added at the side for the giver’s part, 授. So 受 is not passive, like “to suffer” or “to be blamed”. It is the active half of a handing-over: someone holds out the vessel, and the ruler puts out both hands. Our “take on” tries to keep that. The dirt of the state is offered every day. The verse asks who will hold out their hands for it.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 𠬪部: 受，相付也。从𠬪，舟省聲。
Shuowen Jiezi, 手部: 授，予也。从手从受，受亦聲。

gou.title: 垢: the ruler holds dirt in the mouth
gou.body: 垢 is dirt: grime on skin, mud in water. The Shuowen says 濁也, “turbid”, and the graph has 土, earth, on its left. English versions write “disgrace”, “humiliation”, or “blame”, and the link to the first half is cut. The first half is about water, and water takes the dirt: it runs to the lowest place, and everything that is washed ends in it. The verse had a known relative. In 594 BCE, the Zuo chronicle tells, a minister of Jin quoted a saying to his lord: 川澤納汙，山藪藏疾，瑾瑜匿瑕，國君含垢，天之道也. “Rivers and marshes take in filth; mountains and thickets hide harmful things; fine jade hides its flaws; the ruler of a state holds dirt in the mouth. This is heaven’s way.” The ruler is listed with the marsh. What is the “dirt” of a group that you belong to, and where does it now collect?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 土部: 垢，濁也。从土后聲。

gou-variant.title: Dirt, or insult? And a forbidden name
gou-variant.body: A modern collated edition of the Mawangdui silk texts reads 受邦之詬. Two words differ. First, 詬 for 垢. The two graphs share the sound-part 后 and differ in the other half: 垢 has earth, and 詬 has 言, speech. The Shuowen defines 詬 as 恥, shame: it is abuse that is spoken. In the silk version the ruler takes the insults of the state: the curses of the people in a bad year. Early scribes often wrote one of such a pair for the other, so we cannot be sure which word was meant. The received graph keeps the tie to water; the silk graph is closer to politics. Second, 邦 for 國. Both mean “state”. 邦 was the personal name of the first Han emperor, Liu Bang, and after his reign scribes replaced it with 國 through the whole book. The same kind of taboo changed the first line of passage 1.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 言部: 詬，謑詬，恥也。从言后聲。

sheji.title: 社稷: soil and millet
sheji.body: 社 is the altar of the soil, which the Shuowen defines as 地主, “lord of the earth”, and 稷 is the altar of millet, which the Shuowen calls 五穀之長, “the chief of the five grains”. Each state had the pair, beside the ruler’s residence: an open mound of earth for the god of that land, and a place of offering to the grain that fed it. Open is important. An old ritual text says that the altar of a conquered state was roofed over, so that it would no longer receive the light of heaven. To found a state was to raise these altars, and to destroy one was to cover them. So 社稷 came to mean the state itself, more than any ruler; Mencius ranks the people first, the altars second, and the ruler last. 社稷主 is the one who presides at the offerings. The verse says who that is: the person who receives the dirt. Soil is, after all, what the first altar is made of.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 示部: 社，地主也。从示、土。
Shuowen Jiezi, 禾部: 稷，𪗉也。五穀之長。

bu-xiang.title: 不祥, and a king in the mulberry grove
bu-xiang.body: 祥 has 礻, the altar sign, beside 羊, a sheep, the animal of offering. The Shuowen defines it as 福, blessing. 不祥 are the bad signs: eclipse, flood, drought, a strange birth. They were read as heaven’s warning to a state. Who answers for them? The founding story of the Shang dynasty gives the model. After King Tang took the throne, no rain fell for years. Tang went to the mulberry grove, cut off his hair, and offered himself as the victim. His prayer survives in several old books; the Analects gives it so: 朕躬有罪，無以萬方；萬方有罪，罪在朕躬. “If I myself have guilt, do not hold the ten thousand regions to it. If the ten thousand regions have guilt, the guilt rests on me.” The rain came. For centuries afterwards, emperors answered a disaster with an edict that blamed themselves.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 示部: 祥，福也。从示，羊聲。一云善。

wang.title: Lord of one state, king of all
wang.body: The verse has two steps. The one who takes the state’s dirt is 社稷主, lord of one state’s altars. The one who takes its ill omens is 天下王, king of all under heaven. In the Warring States that second title was the prize of the age. Seven rulers called themselves 王, and each hoped to be the one king. The books of strategy told them how: armies, alliances, grain. The verse gives another qualification, and it has nothing to do with force. The Shuowen defines 王 by a word of like sound, 往: 天下所歸往也, “the one to whom all under heaven go home”. Passage 66 uses the word of water: the rivers and the sea can be 王 of the hundred valleys because they lie below them. So “king” here is less a rank than a low point, where everything arrives. English “king” has a throne under it. This one has a valley floor.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 王部: 王，天下所歸往也。

gu-gua.title: Orphan, widowed, grainless
gu-gua.body: The verse describes a habit that every reader of the time knew from court speech. A ruler did not say “I”. He called himself 孤, the orphan; 寡人, the lonely or deficient one; or 不穀, “the one without grain”, the unfruitful. The Laozi points to this twice: these are the names that people most hate, and lords and kings take them as their titles (39, 42). So the grammar of rule already contained the idea of the verse: the highest person carries the lowest names. By the Warring States the names were only etiquette, and a king who called himself “the orphan” could tax his people to starvation, as passage 75 says. The verse asks for the content behind the title. What would change if the humble words that leaders use, “I serve”, “I take full responsibility”, were taken as literal?

scapegoat.title: Not a scapegoat, not “responsibility”
scapegoat.body: Two Western frames press on this verse, and both bend it. The first is religious: the scapegoat that carries the people’s sins into the desert, and the servant who has “borne our griefs”. In those pictures the bearer is driven out or killed, and the guilt goes away with him. The Chinese ruler is not removed. He stays, and the dirt stays in him, as silt stays in a lake. Nothing is redeemed. It is held. The second frame is managerial: “the leader takes responsibility”. That is an office phrase, and it is often a prelude to a statement and a clean exit. 垢 is not a statement. It is the mud itself: the failures, the hatred, the things that no one will touch. The verse does not say that taking it is noble. It says that this, and nothing finer, is what the word “lord” means.

zheng-yan.title: 正言若反: the book names its method
zheng-yan.body: Four characters close the passage: straight words, like, reversed. 正 is upright and correct, the word for a line that is true. 反 is a thing turned over; the Shuowen says 覆也. The sentence is a reader’s guide to the whole book, placed three passages before the end. The weak wins. The low is king. The one who knows does not speak. Each of these sounds upside down, and the text says: that is how straight speech sounds to a bent ear. Two earlier lines stand behind it. 反者道之動, “turning back is the movement of Dao” (40); there 反 is what Dao does. And passage 41 lists a row of “seems”: the bright way seems dim, the way forward seems to go back. 若 is “seems”, and it matters. The words are not reversed. They seem so, from where we stand. What would you have to change for them to sound straight?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 又部: 反，覆也。

legge.title: Legge’s hymn
legge.body: Legge saw that the sage’s saying was verse, and he gave it rhyme and metre: “He who accepts his state’s reproach, / Is hailed therefore its altars’ lord; / To him who bears men’s direful woes / They all the name of King accord.” It is an English hymn stanza. 垢, dirt, is “reproach”, a word from the Psalms. 不祥, bad omens, are “men’s direful woes”, and the verb is “bears”: a nineteenth-century churchgoer hears the suffering servant at once. “King” has a capital. Legge added a crowd that hails and accords; the Chinese has only 是謂, “this is called”. He ends: “Words that are strictly true seem to be paradoxical”, which is fair, and his “paradoxical” is Greek for the same thought: against opinion. His first sentence shows less ease. For [[其無以易之|yi]] he gives two readings joined by a dash, and adds “(so effectual)” in brackets.
src: James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Sacred Books of the East vol. 39 (1891)

low-water.title: Be the low place once
low-water.body: In any group, some things roll downhill until they find a person: the task that no one wants, the complaint with no clear owner, the fault that belongs to everyone a little. Most of us step aside by reflex. Once this week, when such a thing rolls toward you, hold out your hands. Say “give it to me”, or simply take it, and add no speech about it. Then observe three things. First, what the others do: often the room relaxes, as ground drains when it has an outlet. Second, what your body does: the pull to explain, to mention that it was not your fault. Third, whether you can let the dirt settle in you without becoming dirty in your own eyes. Water that takes mud is still water. Do not do this every time. The verse describes a ruler, and one must know the size of one’s lake.

lenses.ground: The passage has two halves and a last line. The first half is about [[water|shui]]: nothing is softer or weaker, and nothing is better at [[the assault|gong]] on hard things, because [[nothing can take its place|yi]]. Then the general rule, weak over strong and soft over [[hard|gang]], with a dry remark: [[everyone knows it and no one can walk it|mo]]. The second half is [[a rhymed saying|yun]] about rulers. To [[receive|shou]] the state’s [[dirt|gou]] is to be lord of its [[altars|sheji]]; to receive its [[ill omens|bu-xiang]] is to be [[king|wang]]. The link between the halves is not stated. It is in the image: water runs to the lowest place and takes everything that is washed down. The ruler is that low water. The last line, [[straight words seem turned around|zheng-yan]], comments on this passage and on the book.
lenses.inner: Everyone knows, no one can walk it. Why not? Because to be soft and low in fact, and not only in theory, one must receive what the low place receives. In a person this is the material that the mind sends away: shame, failure, the envy that one denies, the old injury. The usual inner government is hard: it keeps a clean image by pushing the dirt out, onto others or out of sight. The verse describes another government. The one who can [[take the dirt|gou]] into awareness and hold it, without washing it off and without drowning in it, becomes master of the whole inner state, because nothing in it is any longer in exile. This is [[not redemption|scapegoat]]. The mud is not turned into gold. It settles. Still water with silt at the bottom is clear at the top.
lenses.leading: The verse is the book’s shortest definition of legitimacy. Authority belongs to the one who receives what the group cannot bear to hold: its failures and its bad luck. Court language already said so in its forms, since rulers called themselves [[the orphan and the grainless|gu-gua]]; the text asks that the form be filled. The model is [[King Tang in the mulberry grove|bu-xiang]]: the guilt of the ten thousand regions rests on me. Note the two levels. To take the dirt, the internal faults, makes one fit to lead a group. To take the ill omens, the blows from outside that are no one’s fault, makes one fit for [[more than a group|wang]]. Note also what the modern phrase [[“taking responsibility”|scapegoat]] leaves out: the ruler in the verse does not resign afterwards. Try [[the low place|low-water]] once before you judge the idea.
lenses.body: Water’s way of attack is a lesson in contact. It does not strike a wall. It leans on it with its whole weight, finds each crack, and stays. In the soft martial arts this is called sticking and following: the hand rests on the partner’s arm, heavy and without force, and goes where the arm goes. The partner pushes and meets nothing hard; the pressure only arrives somewhere else. To do this the body must [[receive|shou]]. A push is taken in through the arms, down the spine, and into the ground, as a low field takes rain. The beginner’s body refuses and braces; that is 剛. Stand with a partner and let them push your shoulder slowly. Do not resist and do not collapse. Let the push drain through you to your feet. Everyone knows this, and to do it takes years.
lenses.nature: A gorge is the plain proof of the first lines. A river with no edge cut it through rock, and it used the rock’s own grit as its teeth. Water does this by being [[what nothing can replace|yi]]: it keeps its nature at every point, and it never stops arriving. The second half of the passage is also in the landscape. Follow any stream down and you reach a marsh, a delta, a lake bed. All the dirt of the country ends there: silt, leaves, the waste of towns. These low, muddy places are the most fertile ground on earth, and the early states of China grew on river silt. The saying in the Zuo chronicle puts [[the ruler beside the marsh|gou]] for this reason. In the living world, to receive the dirt is the start of soil. The first altar of a state was [[a mound of earth|sheji]].
lenses.practice: Use water today as a teacher, twice. First, with the hands: when you wash something, watch what the water does. It does not scrub. It takes the dirt into itself and carries it down, and the thing is clean because the water agreed to be dirty. Second, with people: [[be the low place once|low-water]]. When a small blame is in the air and looking for someone, receive it, even if only a tenth of it is yours, and say nothing in your defence. Feel how much effort the usual defence costs. In the evening, read the last line again, 正言若反, and pick one sentence from this book that sounded upside down when you first met it. Does it [[still seem reversed|zheng-yan]]? Then compare the saying with [[Legge’s hymn stanza|legge]].

plates.title: Earth beside a sovereign
plates.lesson: Two parts, side by side. On the left is 土, earth. The Shuowen says of it 地之吐生物者也, “that part of the ground which puts forth living things”, and it reads the two level strokes as the surface and the depth of the ground, with the upright as a thing that comes out. On the right is 后 (hòu), which gives the sound. And here a reader of this passage should stop, because 后 is a word for a ruler. The Shuowen defines it as 繼體君也, “the lord who continues the line”, the sovereign who 施令以告四方, “issues commands to inform the four quarters”. It is the title in 后稷, Lord Millet, the ancestor of the Zhou house, and later it became the word for a queen. So the character for dirt is written “earth” and “sovereign”. The dictionary treats this as sound only: 从土后聲. No one planned a meaning. But the passage says that the one who receives 垢 is lord of the altars, and the altar of the soil is a mound of 土. The graph happens to hold the whole verse. Its sister 詬, with speech in place of earth, means spoken abuse; [[the collated silk text has that graph here|gou-variant]]. Others with the same sound-part are 逅, a meeting by chance, and 姤, the hexagram of meeting. As for the meaning, the Shuowen says 濁也: turbid, like water that carries earth. That is [[the first half of the passage|gou]] in one word.
plates.brush: Nine strokes: three for earth, six for the sovereign. Earth at the left is narrow: a short level line, an upright through it, and then a base stroke that does not lie flat. It rises to the right, like a flick. This is the rule for 土 on the left side; the rising stroke makes room and points to the next part. Now 后. Its first stroke is a short flat slash across the top, written from right to left. Its second is a long slash that starts under the first and falls far to the lower left; give it a slow curve. Third, a level line that starts at that long stroke and runs right. Then the mouth in three strokes: left side, top and right side with a corner, base. Keep the mouth small and low, under the level line. The long slash is the roof of the whole right side.

plates.title: The lizard of change
plates.lesson: The Shuowen begins its entry with three names of one small animal: 蜥易，蝘蜓，守宮也, the lizard, the gecko, the “palace guard” that lives on house walls. Then it says 象形, “a picture”: the top part is the head, and the lower strokes are the legs and tail. On this account 易, the word for change, is a lizard, an animal that tradition says changes its colour through the day, and the creature itself was later written with an insect sign added: 蜴. The Shuowen then records a second opinion from a book of secret lore: 日月爲易，象陰陽也, “sun and moon make 易; it pictures yin and yang”. In the modern shape you can indeed see 日, the sun, on top, and with good will a moon below. Modern scholars doubt both stories. The oldest forms are commonly explained as liquid poured from one vessel into another: an exchange. The three senses of the word follow from any of these pictures. To change. To exchange one thing for another, which is [[the sense that Wang Bi takes in this passage|yi]]. And easy: what changes without resistance. The same graph names the Book of Changes, 易經. Its family keeps the sound: 賜, to bestow, with a shell; 錫, tin, with metal; 踢, to kick, with a foot. Water is the best 易 thing in the world, and the line says that nothing can 易 it.
plates.brush: Eight strokes: four above, four below. The upper part is written as 日, the sun: left side down; top and right side in one stroke with a corner; the inner level line; the base that closes it. Keep it flat and compact, a little narrower than what comes next. The lower part begins with a slash that falls left from under the box. The sixth stroke is the important one: it goes right, turns a corner, comes down with a slight curve inward, and ends in a hook. Inside its curve go two more slashes, parallel, both falling to the left. The three slashes must not be equal. Write the first short, the second longer, the third longest, like the legs of an animal seen from the side. In cursive script the whole lower part becomes one spiral.

plates.title: The flame in the lamp
plates.lesson: This plain character, 王 with a dot on top, is one of the surprises of the Shuowen. Its definition is 鐙中火主也, “the flame in the middle of a lamp”. The lower part is the lamp: a stand with a bowl for the oil. The dot at the top is the flame, and the Shuowen says that the dot is also the sound and the root of the word; it explains 丶 by itself as the mark that a reader makes at a stopping place, a small point of ink. So 主 began as the point of fire at the centre of a dark room. From there the sense grew by a clear path. The flame is what the room gathers around, so 主 is the host as against the guest, the owner as against the borrower, the lord as against the subject, and the main point as against the side issues. When the word had taken on these senses, the lamp wick got a new graph with fire added: 炷. The family shares the idea of a fixed point: 住, to stay, with a person; 柱, a pillar, with wood; 注, to pour onto one spot, with water; 駐, to halt a horse. Do not confuse 主 with 王, the king, which the Shuowen explains as three lines joined by one, though the two meet in this verse: 社稷主 and 天下王. The lord of the altars is, by the old picture, a small flame. A flame gives light because it [[accepts to burn|shou]].
plates.brush: Five strokes. First the dot: set the brush down at the top centre, press to the lower right, and lift. It should sit clear of the line below and not touch it. Then three level lines and an upright, in this order: the first level line; the second, shorter; then the upright, from the first line down through the second; and last the long base, which closes the foot. Space the three level lines evenly and make the base the widest. Everything hangs from the dot, so its place decides whether the character stands straight; a dot too far left makes the lamp lean. In seal script the top is a small upright tongue of flame and the body below is clearly a stand with a bowl. Regular script reduced the flame to one touch of the brush tip.
